---
title: "Phones and saves"
subtitle: "Touch controls that survive real phones, and settings that survive a reload."
---

[Lesson 10](../lessons/10-ship.qmd) gave *Cold Chain* a floating joystick and a saved best time. *Snail Assassin* goes further on both, and its code comments say why: each extra piece is a fix for something that went wrong on a real device.

## More than a joystick

{{< snippet repo="minus80" file="snail-assassin/src/input/TouchControls.ts" lines="20-27" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Three ways to move and aim, because a snail game is played slowly and deliberately:

- a **joystick** on the left, like *Cold Chain*'s;
- **hold to crawl**: press and hold anywhere on the reef, and after 220 ms the snail crawls toward your finger, so one finger is enough to play;
- **tap to aim**: a quick tap sets where abilities fire.

The last paragraph of that comment is the kind of thing you only learn by testing on phones: mobile Safari doesn't always send `pointermove` and `pointerup` events reliably, so the controls read the pointers' positions every frame instead of waiting for events. *Cold Chain*'s `TouchStick` relies on those events, which is fine for a course game and worth knowing before you ship one.
:::

## One input, many devices

{{< snippet repo="minus80" file="snail-assassin/src/scenes/HuntScene.ts" lines="186-189" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
The keyboard produces a `HuntInput`. Touch takes that and overrides what it needs. The accessibility assist takes the result and adjusts the aim. The hunt only ever sees one `HuntInput`, and never knows which device it came from. That's the same idea as *Cold Chain*'s direction vector ([lesson 10](../lessons/10-ship.qmd#touch)), extended to every action.

There's also a safety net in `create()`: some browsers don't say they support touch until the first touch, so the game turns touch controls on at the first `pointerdown` that `wasTouch`.
:::

## Full screen, where allowed

{{< snippet repo="minus80" file="snail-assassin/src/ui/fullscreen.ts" method="toggleFullscreen" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`startFullscreen` hides the browser's bars on Android, tablets and desktops. On a phone, it then asks to lock the screen sideways; if the browser says no, `.catch(() => undefined)` quietly ignores it. iPhones don't allow full screen for web pages at all, so the game also ships a web app manifest: "Add to Home Screen" opens it full screen and sideways.
:::

## Settings that survive

{{< snippet repo="minus80" file="snail-assassin/src/config/settings.ts" lines="41-83" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Everything [lesson 10](../lessons/10-ship.qmd#remember-things) asked for, in one place:

- **One key, namespaced**: `minus80.snail-assassin.settings`, so the studio's other games on the same site can't clash with it.
- **One object, as JSON.** All settings are saved together, and loaded over the defaults (`{ ...current, ...saved }`), so a setting added in a later version gets its default value instead of `undefined`.
- **Every access wrapped in `try`**, with a comment saying what happens if storage is blocked.
- **Loaded once, then cached** in `current`, so the game doesn't read storage every frame.

`markOnce` records that you've seen something (the tutorial, a science reveal) so it can be skipped next time: [exercise 7.4](../lessons/07-scenes.qmd#exercises)'s "tutorial finished", built.
:::
